currentUse: Sacred Heart Parish merged in 2008 with Holy Family of New Philadelphia and St. Anthony of Cumbola to form Holy Cross Parish. Holy Cross worships at the former Holy Family site, so it is a distinct merger successor and not a renaming of Sacred Heart. The former Sacred Heart church on Clay Street, a building dedicated in 1984, remains standing and has been reported in field survey use as a church-owned weekly café. Current access and the café's 2026 operating status have not been independently confirmed.
summary: Sacred Heart was New Philadelphia's Lithuanian Roman Catholic parish. The Sacred Heart Lithuanian Society organized about 1892, met in the public school, and began focused parish organizing in 1894. In autumn 1895 the Archbishop of Philadelphia authorized a Lithuanian parish and appointed Father V. Matulaitis, who served it from Minersville. After temporary worship in the Irish church and public-school rooms, parishioners built a small church, acquired a cemetery in 1898, and completed a larger church beside the first structure in 1902. The church was enlarged in 1915, and a parish school and convent opened in 1926. A new church was dedicated on Clay Street in 1984. In 2008 Sacred Heart merged with two neighboring parishes to form Holy Cross, which worships at the former Holy Family site. The 1984 Sacred Heart building stands separately from that institutional succession and has been reported repurposed as a church-owned café.

historicalNarrative.text: The parish grew from the Sacred Heart Lithuanian Society, organized about 1892. Members met monthly in the New Philadelphia public school and attended the local Irish Catholic church, where Father Simon Pautienius of Mahanoy City periodically heard confessions and preached in Lithuanian. The society began serious parish planning in May 1894. In autumn 1895 the Archbishop of Philadelphia granted permission to organize a Lithuanian parish and appointed Father V. Matulaitis of Minersville to serve it. This establishes 1895 as the parish's foundation, distinct from the earlier society phase.

historicalNarrative.text: Father Matulaitis continued to reside at the Minersville rectory and traveled to New Philadelphia each Sunday. After the Lithuanian group lost use of the Irish church, it worshiped in public-school rooms until parishioners completed a small church costing about $2,000. The cemetery was acquired in 1898. In spring 1901 Father A. Kaminskas broke ground for a larger church beside the first structure; basement services began that autumn, and the church was completed in 1902 at a cost of about $15,000. These successive worship sites must not be compressed into the later 1984 building.

historicalNarrative.text: The 1902 church was enlarged in 1915. In 1925 the parish broke ground for a combined school and convent; the school began its first year in fall 1926 with 346 students taught by the Sisters of St. Casimir, and its cornerstone was blessed that October. Borough history records a new Sacred Heart church dedicated on Clay Street in 1984. The school, cemetery, older church phases, and 1984 church are related parts of the parish complex but have separate physical histories.

historicalNarrative.text: In 2008 Sacred Heart, Holy Family of New Philadelphia, and St. Anthony of Cumbola merged to form Holy Cross Parish. Holy Cross uses the former Holy Family building, so the relationship is an institutional merger into a distinct successor without retention of the Sacred Heart church as the successor's worship site. The 1984 Sacred Heart building on Clay Street remains standing and a later field survey reported church-owned café use. That hosted commercial use does not continue Sacred Heart as a parish.

conflictsWithArchiveRecord: The parish-produced jubilee establishes 1895 as the foundation year; 1892 is the predecessor society's formation, not the parish date. The church sequence includes a first small church, a 1901–1902 replacement enlarged in 1915, and a 1984 church. The 2008 event is an institutional merger into Holy Cross, whose worship site is former Holy Family; the standing former Sacred Heart building and its later café use are separate building-history facts.
gaps: Street numbers for the first church, 1902 church, rectory, and school; the exact 1984 dedication date and full address; the 2008 decree and effective date; sacramental-record custody; cemetery ownership; and the former church's current owner, café name, public access, and 2026 operating status remain unresolved. The 1984 building is securely located on Clay Street, with civic map sources also placing it along Wiggan Street, but a numbered postal address has not been verified.
